title: In a café: ordering drinks (Im Café)
summary: Order a drink or a piece of cake politely with Ich möchte ... and Ich hätte gern ..., and ask a friend what they'd like.
goals: Order a drink or a piece of cake politely
Ask what someone would like: Was möchtest du?
Use einen, eine, ein when you order

nicosWeg.title: Nicos Weg A1, chapter 3: In company (Was trinkst du?, Eine Pizza bitte!)

sections.title: Three ways to order
sections.text:
In a café you can order in three ways, from short to polite:
- [[Einen Kaffee, bitte.]] Short and completely normal.
- [[Ich möchte einen Kaffee.]] = I'd like a coffee.
- [[Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee.]] = I'd like a coffee. A little more polite; you may know it from the Extras page.

The waiter or the person at the counter asks [[Was möchten Sie?]] or [[Was darf es sein?]] (What can I get you? [[darf]] comes in Unit 5). A friend asks [[Was möchtest du trinken?]]

[[trinken]] (to drink) you know from the song 'Sieben Tage lang'.

[[möchten]] works like the verbs from Unit 3 ([[können]], [[wollen]], [[müssen]]): [[ich]] and [[er]]/[[sie]]/[[es]] have the same form, [[möchte]], with no -t (not 'er möchtet'), and a second verb goes to the end: [[Ich möchte bezahlen.]] [[Was möchtest du trinken?]]

sections.title: einen, eine, ein when you order
sections.text:
You know from Unit 2 that masculine [[ein]] becomes [[einen]] after [[haben]] and [[brauchen]]. The same happens when you order, after [[möchten]] and [[hätte gern]], and also in the short version with just [[bitte]]:
- [[der Kaffee]]: [[Einen Kaffee, bitte.]]
- [[die Tasse]]: [[Eine Tasse Tee, bitte.]]
- [[das Bier]]: [[Ein Bier, bitte.]]

Only the masculine changes. Lesson 2 shows the whole pattern. [[mit Milch]] (with milk) is a chunk; Unit 6 explains [[mit]]. In speech you'll also hear [[Ein Kaffee, bitte.]]: people say it, and you'll be understood either way.

German puts the amount and the drink side by side, with no 'of' and no change: [[ein Glas Wasser]], [[eine Tasse Tee]]. Armenian does the same (մի բաժակ ջուր), but Russian changes the drink: стакан воды, чашка чая. So don't look for a Russian genitive here.
Remember Unit 3: [[Ich will einen Kaffee.]] sounds like a child or a boss. Order with [[Ich möchte ...]] or [[Ich hätte gern ...]].

sections.title: In a Munich beer garden
sections.text: Beer often comes in big glasses: [[eine Maß]] is one litre, [[eine Halbe]] half a litre. [[Eine Maß, bitte!]] is a complete order.

items.de: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee mit Milch.
items.en: I'd like a coffee with milk.
Would you like some cake too?

items.de: Ja, gern. Ein Stück Kuchen, bitte.
items.en: Yes, please. A piece of cake, please.
What would you like to drink?

items.instruction: Fill in the gap: I'd like a tea, please.
items.explanation: ich möchte: the same form as er möchte, with no -t.

items.instruction: Fill in the gap: I'd like a coffee.
items.explanation: der Kaffee is masculine, so einen Kaffee, as after haben.

items.question: Which order sounds polite?
items.explanation: Ich hätte gern ... (or Ich möchte ...) is the polite way. Ich will ... sounds pushy.

items.instruction: Fill in the gap: What would you like to drink? (informal)
items.explanation: du möchtest. trinken waits at the end, as after a modal verb.
ein Glas Wasser: no 'of' in German. das Glas, so ein.
